meta.description: Combined AIBE question pool across multiple subjects, for mixed-subject mock exams. Each question tagged with its source subject and that subject's real AIBE weightage (approx. questions out of 100 in the actual exam).

questions.q: The words "SOCIALIST," "SECULAR," and "INTEGRITY" were inserted into the Preamble by which Amendment?
questions.src: The 42nd Amendment Act 1976, often called the "Mini-Constitution," inserted these words into the Preamble.

questions.q: Article 19(1) of the Constitution guarantees how many distinct freedoms?
questions.src: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms: speech/expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession/trade/business.

questions.q: The grounds of prohibited discrimination under Article 15(1) are:
o: Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, and age
Religion, race, caste, sex, and place of birth
Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, and residence
questions.src: Article 15(1) lists exactly five grounds — religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth — and notably does NOT include age or residence.

questions.q: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that "procedure established by law" under Article 21 must be:
o: Simply any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, regardless of fairness
FAIR, JUST, and REASONABLE, not merely enacted
Only applicable to citizens, never foreigners
questions.src: Maneka Gandhi read substantive due process into Article 21, requiring the procedure itself to be fair, just, and reasonable.

questions.q: Article 21A (Right to Education) was inserted by which Amendment, and covers which age group?
questions.src: The 86th Amendment 2002 inserted Article 21A, guaranteeing free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14.

questions.q: A person arrested must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within how many hours under Article 22?
questions.src: Article 22 requires production before a Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time necessary for travel from the place of arrest.

questions.q: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar referred to which Article as "the heart and soul of the Constitution"?
questions.src: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) was famously described by Ambedkar in these terms.

questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are:
o: Fully enforceable by courts, exactly like Fundamental Rights
NON-JUSTICIABLE, yet declared fundamental in the governance of the country under Article 37
Only applicable during a national emergency
questions.src: DPSPs are expressly non-justiciable under Article 37, though declared fundamental to governance.

questions.q: The writ of "Certiorari" is used to:
o: Prevent a proceeding before it concludes
QUASH a decision already made by a subordinate court/tribunal acting without or in excess of jurisdiction
Compel performance of a public duty
Challenge unlawful occupation of public office
questions.src: Certiorari is corrective — it quashes an already-made decision, distinct from Prohibition's preventive function.

questions.q: Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction), compared to Article 32 (Supreme Court), is generally:
o: WIDER — covering Fundamental Rights AND "any other purpose"
Not applicable to Fundamental Rights at all
questions.src: Article 226's "any other purpose" language gives it broader scope than Article 32.

questions.q: The word "internal disturbance" in Article 352 was replaced with "armed rebellion" by which Amendment?
questions.src: The 44th Amendment 1978, responding to the 1975 Emergency's misuse, made this change.

questions.q: "Financial Emergency" under Article 360, in India's constitutional history to date, has been:
questions.src: Article 360 remains a purely theoretical provision, never formally proclaimed in India.

questions.q: Under Article 368, amendments affecting the federal structure (e.g., Article 368 itself, Presidential election) require:
o: Special majority PLUS ratification by at least one-half of State Legislatures
Only Presidential assent, no Parliamentary vote
questions.src: This third, most stringent amendment mode protects genuinely federal-structure-affecting provisions.

questions.q: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Basic Structure Doctrine was established by a bench of how many judges, with what majority?
questions.src: This remains the largest Constitution Bench in Indian history, deciding by a narrow 7:6 majority.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly represents the chronological sequence of the Basic Structure case law?
o: Kesavananda Bharati → Golaknath → Shankari Prasad → Minerva Mills
Shankari Prasad → Golaknath → Kesavananda Bharati → Minerva Mills
Minerva Mills → Kesavananda Bharati → Golaknath → Shankari Prasad
Golaknath → Shankari Prasad → Minerva Mills → Kesavananda Bharati
questions.src: The correct chronological sequence is Shankari Prasad (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980).

questions.q: The Ninth Schedule, which shields specified laws from Fundamental-Rights-based judicial review, was added by:
questions.src: The Ninth Schedule was added by the very first constitutional amendment in 1951.

questions.q: Following I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are:
o: Completely immune from judicial review under all circumstances
STILL reviewable if they damage the Constitution's Basic Structure
questions.src: I.R. Coelho clarified that Ninth Schedule protection does not extend to laws that violate the Basic Structure.

questions.q: The Tenth Schedule, dealing with Anti-Defection provisions, was added by which Amendment?
questions.src: The 52nd Amendment 1985 inserted the Tenth Schedule governing disqualification for defection.

questions.q: The Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules, dealing with Panchayat and Municipality powers respectively, were added by:
questions.src: The 73rd Amendment (Panchayats, Eleventh Schedule) and 74th Amendment (Municipalities, Twelfth Schedule), both 1992, established constitutional status for local self-government.

questions.q: The minimum age to be eligible for election as President of India is:
questions.src: Article 58 sets the minimum age qualification for the Presidency at 35 years.

questions.q: Supreme Court judges retire upon attaining the age of:
questions.src: Supreme Court judges have a retirement age of 65, distinct from High Court judges' retirement age of 62.

questions.q: High Court judges retire upon attaining the age of:
questions.src: High Court judges retire at 62, while Supreme Court judges retire at 65 — a frequently tested distinguishing pair.

questions.q: The National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), introduced by the 99th Amendment 2014, was:
o: Upheld as constitutional and remains in force today
STRUCK DOWN in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case), preserving the Collegium system
Never brought before the Supreme Court
Replaced by a fully executive-controlled appointment system
questions.src: The Fourth Judges Case (2015) struck down the NJAC as violating judicial independence, a Basic Structure feature.

questions.q: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court, while upholding OBC reservation, introduced which important ceiling?
questions.src: The 50% reservation ceiling (with limited later-recognised exceptions) is one of Indra Sawhney's most cited holdings.

questions.q: Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer is generally credited as:
o: The first Chief Justice of independent India
The father of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India
The chairman of the Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee
questions.src: Justice Krishna Iyer is widely regarded as the pioneering figure behind PIL in India, with Justice P.N. Bhagwati also central to its development.

questions.q: In Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that:
o: Right to Privacy is not protected by the Constitution
Right to Privacy IS a Fundamental Right under Article 21
Right to Privacy applies only to public figures
Right to Privacy was left undecided
questions.src: This landmark 9-judge bench ruling firmly established privacy as a Fundamental Right flowing from Article 21.

questions.q: The "Doctrine of Pith and Substance" is used by courts to:
o: Determine the punishment for a criminal offence
Determine the TRUE NATURE of a law when it appears to touch subjects in different Legislative Lists
Calculate compensation in land acquisition cases
questions.src: This doctrine examines a law's true character/substance to determine which legislature validly enacted it, rather than its incidental effects.

questions.q: The "Doctrine of Colourable Legislation" is based on the principle that:
o: A legislature can do indirectly what it cannot do directly, without restriction
What CANNOT be done directly CANNOT be done indirectly — examining legislative competence, not motive
Only the judiciary can enact colourable legislation
It applies exclusively to Money Bills
questions.src: This doctrine focuses on whether a legislature had the constitutional competence to enact a law, regardless of its stated purpose.

questions.q: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court:
o: Upheld Section 377 IPC in its entirety
Read down Section 377 IPC, decriminalising consensual homosexual acts between adults
Struck down the entire Indian Penal Code
Declined to address the constitutional question
questions.src: This landmark ruling decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults by reading down Section 377.

questions.q: In Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), the Supreme Court held that the Right to a SPEEDY TRIAL is:
o: Not part of any constitutional right
Part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21
Only applicable to civil cases, never criminal
A statutory right under the CrPC only, with no constitutional basis
questions.src: This landmark case, concerning undertrial prisoners, established speedy trial as a facet of Article 21.

questions.q: Under which section is a First Information Report (FIR) recorded under BNSS 2023?
questions.src: Section 173 BNSS corresponds to the old Section 154 CrPC -- FIR registration.

questions.q: What was the equivalent provision for FIR registration under the OLD CrPC, 1973?
questions.src: Section 154 CrPC was the FIR provision, now Section 173 under BNSS.

questions.q: Which section provides for Anticipatory Bail under the BNSS?
questions.src: Section 482 BNSS corresponds to Section 438 CrPC -- Anticipatory Bail.

questions.q: Who can grant anticipatory bail?
questions.src: Anticipatory bail can only be granted by the Sessions Court or High Court, never a Magistrate.

questions.q: Under the old CrPC, Section 125 deals with:
o: Maintenance of wives, children, and parents
questions.src: Section 125 CrPC (now Section 144 BNSS) governs maintenance obligations.

questions.q: Under BNSS, arrest without a warrant is governed by which section, corresponding to Section 41 of the old CrPC?
questions.src: Section 35 BNSS corresponds to Section 41 CrPC on arrest without warrant.

questions.q: A person arrested must be produced before a Magistrate within how many hours, excluding travel time?
questions.src: This is a constitutional requirement (Article 22) mirrored in Section 58 BNSS/Section 57 CrPC.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes registration of an FIR for a COGNIZABLE offence?
o: Police may refuse and require a preliminary inquiry first in every case
Registration is MANDATORY -- police cannot refuse (per Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P.)
Only a Magistrate can register an FIR
FIR can only be filed within 24 hours of the offence
questions.src: Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P. (2014) made FIR registration mandatory for cognizable offences, subject to narrow later exceptions.

questions.q: The genuinely NEW "Zero FIR" provision under BNSS allows:
o: FIR to be filed only at the police station with territorial jurisdiction
FIR to be filed at ANY police station regardless of jurisdiction, later transferred to the correct one
FIR to be filed only online
No FIR to be filed for offences committed abroad
questions.src: Zero FIR removes jurisdictional barriers to initial FIR registration, with later transfer to the appropriate police station.

questions.q: For a NON-cognizable offence, the police:
o: Can arrest without a warrant and investigate freely
CANNOT arrest without a warrant, and need the Magistrate's permission before investigating
Have identical powers to cognizable offences
questions.src: Non-cognizable offences require both an arrest warrant AND magisterial permission to investigate, unlike cognizable offences.

questions.q: "Bailable" vs "Non-Bailable" offences, as distinguished from "Cognizable" vs "Non-Cognizable" offences, are:
o: Exactly the same classification under different names
TWO SEPARATE, independent classifications -- a cognizable offence is not automatically non-bailable
questions.src: These are two independent classification systems -- a frequently tested AIBE trap where candidates wrongly assume one from the other.

questions.q: In a BAILABLE offence, bail is:
o: A MATTER OF RIGHT -- the accused must be released on furnishing bail/bond
questions.src: Section 478 BNSS (Section 436 CrPC) makes bail a matter of right in bailable offences.

questions.q: In a NON-BAILABLE offence, bail is:
o: DISCRETIONARY -- granted or refused by the court based on relevant factors
Impossible to obtain under any circumstances
questions.src: Section 480 BNSS (Section 437 CrPC) makes non-bailable offence bail a matter of judicial discretion.

questions.q: "Default Bail" (or "Statutory Bail") arises when:
o: The accused simply requests it verbally
The chargesheet is NOT filed within the statutory 60 or 90-day period
The accused has a clean prior record
questions.src: Section 187 BNSS (Section 167(2) CrPC) creates a statutory right to bail if investigation/chargesheet filing exceeds the prescribed period.

questions.q: Under the genuinely NEW Section 479 BNSS, a first-time offender who has served how much of the maximum sentence is entitled to release on bond?
questions.src: Section 479 BNSS entitles first-time offenders to release after serving one-third of the maximum sentence, with the jail superintendent required to apply proactively.

questions.q: Section 479 BNSS's first-time offender release provision does NOT apply to offences punishable with:
o: Any offence whatsoever, it applies universally
questions.src: This important carve-out excludes the most serious offences from the accelerated release mechanism.

questions.q: A confession or statement recorded by a Magistrate is governed under BNSS by which section, corresponding to Section 164 CrPC?
questions.src: Section 183 BNSS corresponds to Section 164 CrPC on Magistrate-recorded confessions/statements.

questions.q: A "Pardon" under Section 343 BNSS (Section 306 CrPC) may be tendered ONLY by:
o: A Chief Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate specifically
questions.src: If tendered by an unauthorised Magistrate, the entire proceeding is VITIATED -- a frequently repeated AIBE trap question.

questions.q: Which of the following classifications was ELIMINATED as a distinct designation under BNSS, unlike the old CrPC?
questions.src: BNSS removed the specific "Metropolitan Magistrate"/"Metropolitan Area" designation that existed for large cities under the old CrPC.

questions.q: A "Warrant Trial" applies to offences punishable with imprisonment:
questions.src: Warrant trials handle more serious offences (over 2 years), distinct from Summons Trials for lesser offences.

questions.q: A "Summons Trial" applies to offences punishable with imprisonment:
questions.src: Summons trials are for relatively minor offences with punishment not exceeding 2 years.

questions.q: In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Supreme Court laid down guidelines primarily addressing:
o: Arrest and custody safeguards to prevent custodial torture
questions.src: D.K. Basu established mandatory safeguards including arrest memos, informing a relative/friend, and medical examination.

questions.q: In Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Arrest must always happen whenever an offence is lawfully alleged
Arrest is NOT mandatory merely because it is lawful -- it must be justified by genuine necessity
questions.src: This case established that arrest requires genuine necessity, not merely legal permissibility -- a principle now reflected in BNSS's arrest-as-exception approach for offences under 7 years.

questions.q: The maxim "Bail is the rule, jail is the exception" is most associated with which case?
o: Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P.
State of Rajasthan v. Balchand alias Baliay (1977)
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P.
questions.src: This foundational principle on personal liberty and bail comes from State of Rajasthan v. Balchand.

questions.q: Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) is significant because it:
o: Called for streamlined, more liberal bail practices, directly influencing BNSS Section 479
Was overturned immediately after being decided
questions.src: This Supreme Court ruling directly shaped the BNSS reform introducing accelerated first-time offender release.

questions.q: The BNSS 2023 contains how many total sections, compared to the CrPC's 484?
questions.src: BNSS has 531 sections, more than the CrPC's 484, reflecting both consolidation and new additions.

questions.q: BNSS 2023 came into force on:
questions.src: BNSS, along with BNS and BSA, came into force on 1 July 2024.

questions.q: Under BNSS, for offences punishable with imprisonment of 3 to 7 years, police may now:
o: Conduct a PRELIMINARY ENQUIRY (with DySP-rank permission) within 14 days before formal FIR registration
Only investigate with a High Court order
questions.src: This is a genuinely new BNSS provision for this specific punishment-severity band, frequently tested as a "what's new" question.

questions.q: The Inherent Powers of the High Court (e.g., to quash an FIR) are governed under BNSS by which section, corresponding to Section 482 CrPC?
questions.src: Section 528 BNSS corresponds to the well-known Section 482 CrPC inherent powers provision.

questions.q: A complainant registering an FIR is entitled to:
o: No copy of the FIR under any circumstances
A FREE COPY of the FIR
A copy only after paying a fee
A copy only if the case goes to trial
questions.src: BNSS confirms the complainant's right to receive a free copy of the registered FIR.

questions.q: Res Judicata is defined under which section of the Code of Civil Procedure?
questions.src: Section 11 CPC codifies the doctrine of Res Judicata.

questions.q: Which section of CPC provides that civil courts have jurisdiction to try all civil suits unless barred?
questions.src: Section 9 establishes the general jurisdiction of civil courts, subject to express/implied bars.

questions.q: "Res Sub Judice" under Section 10 CPC applies when:
o: An earlier suit on the same matter has ALREADY been decided
An earlier suit on the same matter, between the same parties, is still PENDING in a competent court
questions.src: Res Sub Judice (S.10) concerns a PENDING earlier suit, distinct from Res Judicata (S.11) which concerns an already-DECIDED matter.

questions.q: The Latin maxim "interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium" is most directly associated with which CPC doctrine?
questions.src: This maxim ("it is in the interest of the state that there be an end to litigation") underlies the doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11.

questions.q: Under Section 20 CPC, a suit may generally be instituted in a court within whose jurisdiction:
o: The defendant resides/carries on business, OR the cause of action wholly or partly arises
Only the subject property is situated, in every type of suit
questions.src: Section 20 provides the general rule for place of suing, based on defendant's location or where the cause of action arose.

questions.q: Under Section 80 CPC, a suit against the Government generally cannot be instituted until:
o: One month after filing a complaint
The EXPIRATION OF TWO MONTHS after delivering a written notice
Five years after the cause of action arose
questions.src: Section 80 mandates a two-month notice period before suing the Government or a public officer for official acts.

questions.q: Under Order II Rule 2 CPC, if a plaintiff omits to sue for one of several reliefs arising from the same cause of action, they:
o: May always file a fresh suit for the omitted relief later without restriction
Are generally BARRED from a later separate suit for the omitted relief, unless leave of court was obtained
Must always include every possible relief or lose the entire suit
Can only proceed if the defendant consents
questions.src: Order II Rule 2 requires a plaintiff to include their whole claim in one suit, barring most later separate suits for omitted reliefs.

questions.q: Pleadings, under Order VI CPC, must state:
o: The detailed evidence supporting each claim
MATERIAL FACTS, not the evidence by which those facts are to be proved
questions.src: The fundamental rule of pleading requires stating material facts, leaving evidence for the trial stage.

questions.q: Which Order and Rule of CPC governs the AMENDMENT of pleadings?
questions.src: Order VI Rule 17 governs amendment of pleadings, allowing courts to permit changes necessary for determining the real questions in controversy.

questions.q: When deciding an application under Order VII Rule 11 (rejection of plaint), a court may examine:
o: Both the plaint and the defendant's written statement equally
ONLY the averments made in the plaint itself (and documents filed with it)
Only oral evidence presented at trial
Only the opinion of the opposing counsel
questions.src: A classic AIBE trap -- Order VII Rule 11 applications are decided based on the plaint alone, not the defence.

questions.q: In Srihari Hanumandas Totala v. Hemant Vithal Kamat (2021), the Supreme Court held that Res Judicata:
o: Can always be decided through a simple Order VII Rule 11 application
CANNOT be invoked as a ground for rejecting a plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d), since it requires examining the earlier suit's full record
Does not exist as a valid legal doctrine
questions.src: This modern ruling clarified that Res Judicata's complexity exceeds what a bare Rule 11 rejection application can properly resolve.

questions.q: If a written statement is not filed within the prescribed time, under Order VIII Rule 10, the court:
o: Must automatically dismiss the entire suit
MAY pronounce judgment or pass such order as it deems fit
Has no power to act at all
Must wait indefinitely for the written statement
questions.src: Order VIII Rule 10 gives the court discretion to act, including potentially proceeding to judgment, if the written statement is not timely filed.

questions.q: "Set-Off," under Order VIII Rule 6 CPC, allows a defendant to:
o: Raise an entirely unrelated independent claim against the plaintiff
Claim a MONEY debt owed by the plaintiff be adjusted against the plaintiff's claim in the SAME suit
File a completely separate, new lawsuit only
Demand the case be transferred to a different court
questions.src: Set-off specifically involves a money claim being adjusted against the plaintiff's claim within the existing suit.

questions.q: A "Counterclaim," as distinguished from a "Set-off," allows a defendant to:
o: Only claim money debts owed by the plaintiff
Raise their OWN independent claim against the plaintiff, even if UNRELATED to the plaintiff's original claim
Never raise any claim of their own
Only be used in criminal proceedings
questions.src: Counterclaims are broader than set-off, allowing genuinely independent claims regardless of connection to the plaintiff's suit.

questions.q: If the PLAINTIFF fails to appear when the suit is called for hearing (under Order IX), the court may generally:
o: Automatically rule in the plaintiff's favour
Transfer the case to a criminal court
questions.src: Plaintiff non-appearance under Order IX can result in dismissal of the suit.

questions.q: If the DEFENDANT fails to appear while the plaintiff is present (under Order IX), the court may:
o: Proceed EX PARTE, deciding the case without hearing the defendant
Postpone the case for one year automatically
Refer the matter to arbitration compulsorily
questions.src: Defendant non-appearance can lead to an ex parte decree, decided without the defendant's participation.

questions.q: Under Order XXXIX (Temporary Injunctions), courts typically examine which THREE factors?
o: Only the financial status of the parties
Prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury
Only the age of the dispute
Only whether the parties are related
questions.src: These three classic factors form the standard test courts apply when deciding whether to grant a temporary injunction.

questions.q: For breach of a temporary injunction under Order 39, the maximum period of detention in civil prison is:
questions.src: Order 39 Rule 2A prescribes a maximum civil prison detention period of 3 months for breach of an injunction order.

questions.q: For breach of a temporary injunction, the maximum VALIDITY of an attachment order (absent extension) is:
questions.src: The maximum validity period for such an attachment order is generally 1 year, unless extended by the court for good reason.

questions.q: Section 89 CPC provides for reference of a suit, where settlement elements exist, to:
o: Arbitration, Conciliation, Judicial Settlement (including Lok Adalat), or Mediation
No alternative mechanism exists under CPC
questions.src: Section 89 connects CPC directly to the broader ADR framework, offering multiple alternative dispute resolution pathways.

questions.q: Order XXI CPC, one of the longest and most detailed Orders, primarily governs:
o: EXECUTION of decrees -- how a decree-holder actually obtains what the court awarded
questions.src: Order XXI covers the practical mechanics of decree execution, including attachment, sale, and delivery of property.

questions.q: A "Second Appeal" (Sections 100-103 CPC), unlike a First Appeal, may generally be filed only on the ground of:
o: The personal preference of the parties
questions.src: Second Appeal is deliberately restricted to substantial questions of law, distinguishing it from the broader First Appeal.

questions.q: "Revision" under Section 115 CPC refers to:
o: A right of appeal available to any party automatically
The High Court's SUPERVISORY power over subordinate courts acting without or in excess of jurisdiction
A power exercised only by the Supreme Court
An automatic re-trial of every case
questions.src: Revision is a supervisory jurisdiction, distinct from an ordinary right of appeal, focused on jurisdictional errors.

questions.q: "Review" under Section 114 and Order XLVII CPC is decided by:
o: The SAME court that passed the original decree/order, on specified narrow grounds
questions.src: Review is distinctive in being heard by the SAME court, unlike appeal (a different, higher court) or revision (a supervisory court).

questions.q: In Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorjin Debi (1960), the Supreme Court held that Res Judicata:
o: Only applies between two entirely separate lawsuits, never within one case
Applies not only to separate suits but also to DIFFERENT STAGES of the SAME proceeding
Does not apply to civil matters at all
Was abolished by this very judgment
questions.src: This case extended Res Judicata's application to different stages within a single ongoing proceeding, not merely separate suits.

questions.q: In Mathura Prasad v. Dossabhoi N.B. Jeejeebhoy (1970), the Supreme Court held that Res Judicata applies to:
o: Pure questions of law only, never facts
Issues of FACT, not to pure questions of LAW decided in an earlier proceeding
questions.src: This case clarified an important limit on Res Judicata's scope -- it operates on factual issues, not pure legal questions.

questions.q: A civil suit contesting a right to property or a public office is considered a suit of a "civil nature" under Section 9, EVEN IF:
o: The right depends entirely on questions of religious rites or ceremonies
The property value exceeds a certain threshold
The suit is filed after a specified deadline
questions.src: Explanation I to Section 9 specifically confirms this remains a suit of civil nature despite the religious-rites dependency.

questions.q: For IMMOVABLE property specifically, under Section 16 CPC, a suit must generally be filed:
o: Wherever the plaintiff happens to reside
In the court within whose jurisdiction the property is SITUATED
Only in the High Court of the relevant state
Only in Delhi, regardless of property location
questions.src: Section 16 establishes situs-based jurisdiction specifically for suits relating to immovable property.

questions.q: A general or evasive denial in a Written Statement, where specific facts are not clearly addressed, may be treated by the court as:
o: An automatic dismissal of the entire suit
An ADMISSION of the corresponding allegation
Grounds for the plaintiff to be penalised
questions.src: Order VIII's pleading rules mean vague or evasive denials risk being construed as admissions of the plaintiff's allegations.

questions.q: Under Order XL CPC, a court may appoint a Receiver where it appears:
o: Never, this power does not exist under CPC
JUST AND CONVENIENT to preserve/manage disputed property during litigation
Only after the final decree is passed
questions.src: Order XL empowers courts to appoint a Receiver as another form of interim protective relief, distinct from a temporary injunction.

questions.q: Culpable Homicide is defined under Section 100 of the BNS, which corresponds to which section of the old IPC?
questions.src: Section 100 BNS corresponds directly to Section 299 IPC -- the definition of culpable homicide.

questions.q: Murder is defined under Section 101 of the BNS, corresponding to which section of the old IPC?
questions.src: Section 101 BNS corresponds to Section 300 IPC -- the definition of murder as an aggravated species of culpable homicide.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Culpable homicide is the genus, and murder is a species of it. Reason (R): All culpable homicide amounts to murder, and all murder amounts to culpable homicide. Which is correct?
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains (A)
(A) is true, but (R) is FALSE -- not all culpable homicide amounts to murder, though all murder is culpable homicide
questions.src: This is a classic genus-species trap: (A) is correct, but (R) wrongly claims the relationship works in both directions -- it does not.

questions.q: Under Section 101 BNS (Section 300 IPC), Exception 1 (Grave and Sudden Provocation) will NOT apply if:
o: The provocation was genuinely sudden and unexpected
The provocation was SELF-SOUGHT by the offender as an excuse for the killing
The offender had no time to plan the act
The victim was a stranger to the offender
questions.src: One of the key provisos to Exception 1 excludes self-sought or voluntarily provoked provocation used as a pretext.

questions.q: If grave and sudden provocation was given by something done by a public servant in the LAWFUL exercise of their power, Exception 1 to Murder:
o: Applies fully, reducing the offence to culpable homicide
Does NOT apply -- the killing remains MURDER
Applies only if the public servant was off-duty
Is irrelevant to the classification of the offence
questions.src: A specific proviso excludes provocation stemming from a public servant's lawful exercise of power -- Exception 1 fails in this scenario.

questions.q: Under Exception 2 to Murder (Exceeding the Right of Private Defence), the offender's act must be done:
o: With premeditation and intent to cause maximum harm
In GOOD FAITH, WITHOUT premeditation, and without intention of doing more harm than necessary
Only against a stranger, never a family member
questions.src: Exception 2 requires good faith, absence of premeditation, and no intention to exceed necessary harm -- all three conditions must be met.

questions.q: Statement 1: An offender who was the ORIGINAL AGGRESSOR in a confrontation can generally still successfully claim Exception 2 (exceeding private defence). Statement 2: Exception 2 requires the private defence to have been genuinely exercised in good faith. Which is correct?
questions.src: Statement 1 is false -- an original aggressor generally cannot claim private defence at all, defeating Exception 2. Statement 2 correctly reflects the good-faith requirement.

questions.q: Under Exception 5 to Murder (Consent), for this exception to apply, the deceased must have been:
o: Any age, with any form of consent
ABOVE EIGHTEEN years of age, voluntarily consenting to the risk of death or to death itself
A close relative of the accused
questions.src: Exception 5 specifically requires the deceased to be above 18 and to have genuinely, voluntarily consented.

questions.q: Section 103(2) BNS, a GENUINELY NEW provision absent from the original IPC, punishes murder committed by:
o: A GROUP OF FIVE OR MORE persons acting in concert on grounds like caste, race, community, or personal belief (mob lynching)
Only during a declared national emergency
questions.src: Section 103(2) is a new BNS provision specifically targeting group/mob-based murders motivated by identity-based grounds.

questions.q: In Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983), the Supreme Court struck down Section 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for murder by a life-convict) for violating:
questions.src: Mithu held mandatory death sentences with no judicial discretion violate both equality (Art 14) and life/personal liberty (Art 21).

questions.q: In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980), the Supreme Court established the "rarest of rare" doctrine, holding that:
o: Death sentence should be the default rule for all murder convictions
LIFE IMPRISONMENT is the rule for murder, and DEATH SENTENCE the exception, requiring special reasons
All murder convictions require exactly the same sentence
Judicial discretion in sentencing should be entirely eliminated
questions.src: Bachan Singh established that death sentences require special justification, with life imprisonment as the default rule.

questions.q: In Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958), the Supreme Court clarified that for Section 101(c) BNS/Section 300(3) IPC to apply, the prosecution must prove:
o: The accused subjectively intended for the victim to die
The bodily injury inflicted was OBJECTIVELY SUFFICIENT, in the ordinary course of nature, to cause death
The accused had a documented motive for the killing
The victim survived for at least 24 hours after the injury
questions.src: Virsa Singh established an objective sufficiency test, not a subjective intent-to-kill requirement, for this specific murder clause.

questions.q: In K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra (1961), the Supreme Court held that the provocation in question was NOT "sudden" because:
o: The victim provoked the accused repeatedly over many years
There was a TIME GAP allowing the accused's passion to cool before the killing
The accused had no weapon available
The provocation occurred in a public place
questions.src: The time gap allowing for cooling of passion defeated the "sudden" element required for Exception 1 to apply, resulting in a murder conviction.

questions.q: Under the old IPC, Section 303 dealt with "Punishment for Murder by Life Convict." Under the NEW BNS, Section 303 deals with an entirely DIFFERENT offence:
questions.src: A classic trap -- Section 303 has completely different meanings under IPC (murder by life convict, now struck down) versus BNS (theft). Never assume identical section numbers mean identical offences across the two codes.

questions.q: General Exceptions under BNS Chapter III include "Mistake of Fact" -- this excuses an act done by a person:
o: Under a mistake of LAW, regardless of good faith
Bound, or believing in good faith to be bound, by LAW to do it
Only if the mistake benefited a third party
questions.src: Mistake of fact (not mistake of law) can excuse liability, where the person genuinely, reasonably believed they were legally bound/justified.

questions.q: Under Section 20 BNS (General Exceptions), a child UNDER 7 years of age has:
o: Full criminal liability like an adult
ABSOLUTE incapacity -- nothing done by them is an offence
Liability determined case-by-case with no fixed rule
questions.src: Section 20 creates an absolute, irrebuttable incapacity for children under 7.

questions.q: Abetment, under Chapter V BNS, may occur through which THREE means?
o: INSTIGATION, engaging in a CONSPIRACY (with an act/omission in pursuance), or INTENTIONALLY AIDING the commission of the offence
Only if the abettor is present at the scene
questions.src: These are the three recognised means by which a person can abet an offence under the BNS abetment provisions.

questions.q: Under Criminal Conspiracy (Sections 61-62 BNS), for an agreement between two or more persons to constitute the offence, generally:
o: The mere agreement is ALWAYS sufficient regardless of the intended offence
The mere agreement suffices ONLY where the intended offence carries death/life imprisonment/2+ years rigorous imprisonment; OTHERWISE an overt act beyond the agreement is required
No agreement can ever constitute a criminal conspiracy
Only written agreements count as criminal conspiracy
questions.src: This nuanced rule distinguishes serious offences (mere agreement suffices) from lesser offences (an overt act beyond agreement is additionally required).

questions.q: Under Section 62 BNS (the general Attempt provision, corresponding to Section 511 IPC), where an attempted offence is NOT completed, the punishment may extend to:
o: The FULL maximum term for the completed offence
ONE-HALF of the longest term provided for the completed offence, or fine, or both
Double the maximum term as a deterrent
No punishment applies to mere attempts
questions.src: This is the precise numerical formula for general attempt liability -- up to half the maximum term for the completed offence.

questions.q: Assertion (A): BNS has 358 sections across 20 chapters. Reason (R): This represents a significant reduction from the IPC's 511 sections, reflecting consolidation of provisions and removal of obsolete/struck-down sections. Which is correct?
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) does not explain (A)
questions.src: Both statements are accurate, and the reduction genuinely reflects consolidation rather than a narrowing of substantive criminal law coverage.

questions.q: "Kidnapping" under BNS is governed by Section 137, corresponding to which IPC section?
questions.src: Section 137 BNS corresponds to Section 359 IPC on kidnapping.

questions.q: "Abduction" under BNS is governed by Section 138, corresponding to which IPC section?
questions.src: Section 138 BNS corresponds to Section 362 IPC on abduction, distinct from the kidnapping provision.

questions.q: In the general exceptions framework, "Necessity" excuses an act done:
o: In GOOD FAITH to prevent OTHER, greater harm to person or property
Only when no alternative exists whatsoever, with no good faith requirement
questions.src: The necessity exception requires genuine good faith and a real purpose of avoiding greater harm, not a pretext.

questions.q: "Voluntary Intoxication," under the general exceptions framework, is generally treated as:
o: An automatic, complete defence to any criminal charge
NOT a defence generally, though it may be relevant to whether specific intent for certain offences was actually formed
Identical in legal effect to involuntary intoxication
A defence available only to first-time offenders
questions.src: Voluntary intoxication does not generally excuse criminal liability, though courts may consider it in assessing specific intent requirements for particular offences.

questions.q: "Criminal Force," under BNS Section 129 (corresponding to IPC Section 350), as distinguished from "Assault," involves:
o: Only the apprehension of force, not actual contact
The intentional USE of ACTUAL force on another person without consent
Only verbal threats with no physical component
A tort, not a criminal offence
questions.src: Criminal Force involves actual application of force, distinguished from Assault (mere apprehension of imminent force).

questions.q: Under the right of private defence framework (Sections 34-44 BNS), Section 37's restrictions include that the right:
o: Extends without limit to any amount of harm the defender chooses
NEVER extends to inflicting MORE HARM than necessary for the purpose of defence
Applies only to defence of property, never the body
Requires prior police permission before being exercised
questions.src: Section 37 caps the right of private defence, ensuring it never extends beyond what is genuinely necessary for the defensive purpose.

questions.q: Match the following murder-exception scenarios with their correct classification: (i) Offender exceeds private defence in good faith without premeditation (ii) Offender kills after provocation they themselves sought as a pretext (iii) Sudden fight without undue advantage (iv) Deceased, aged 20, voluntarily consented to the risk of death
questions.src: Correctly matching: (i) exceeding private defence = Exception 2; (ii) self-sought provocation defeats Exception 1 entirely; (iii) sudden fight = Exception 4; (iv) valid adult consent = Exception 5.

questions.q: Under Section 105 BNS (Section 304 IPC, Punishment for Culpable Homicide Not Amounting to Murder), the punishment differs based on whether the act was done:
o: On a weekday versus a weekend
With the INTENTION of causing death/likely-fatal injury (higher punishment) versus mere KNOWLEDGE it was likely to cause death without such intention (lower punishment)
By a first-time versus repeat offender only
questions.src: Section 105 BNS prescribes two distinct punishment tiers based on whether intention or mere knowledge was the operative mental element.

questions.q: "Grievous Hurt" under BNS (corresponding to IPC Section 320) includes categories such as:
o: Any momentary bodily discomfort, however minor
Emasculation, permanent privation of sight/hearing, fracture/dislocation of a bone, or hurt causing severe pain/inability to pursue ordinary activities for 20 days
Only hurt caused by a specifically named weapon
Only hurt resulting in immediate death
questions.src: Grievous Hurt is a specifically enumerated, more serious category of hurt than the ordinary threshold, covering these listed severe categories.

questions.q: Statement 1: Attempt to Murder (Section 109 BNS/Section 307 IPC) requires that death actually resulted from the accused's act. Statement 2: An attempt to murder can be punished even where the intended victim survives the attack. Which is correct?
questions.src: Statement 1 is false -- attempt to murder specifically does NOT require death to have occurred (if it did, the offence would be murder itself, not attempt). Statement 2 is correct -- the offence is complete even if the victim survives.

questions.q: Section 26 BSA (Dying Declaration) corresponds to which section of the old Indian Evidence Act?
questions.src: Section 26 BSA corresponds directly to Section 32(1) IEA -- the dying declaration provision.

questions.q: The discovery-from-confession provision (old Section 27 IEA) now corresponds to which BSA section?
questions.src: Section 23 BSA corresponds to the old Section 27 IEA discovery provision.

questions.q: Electronic evidence, formerly governed primarily by Section 65B of the IEA, is now governed by which BSA section?
questions.src: Section 57 BSA replaces the old Section 65B IEA, simplifying the electronic evidence certification procedure.

questions.q: The Burden of Proof framework (old Sections 101-114 IEA) now begins at which BSA section?
questions.src: Sections 104 onwards in the BSA deal with burden of proof, corresponding to the old Sections 101-114 IEA.

questions.q: The total number of sections in the BSA, compared to the old IEA's 167 sections, is:
questions.src: The BSA has 170 sections, a modest increase from the IEA's 167, reflecting reorganization and expansion of electronic evidence provisions.

questions.q: Under Section 3 BSA (the foundational admissibility rule), evidence may be given only of:
o: Any fact whatsoever the parties wish to raise
Facts in issue AND facts declared relevant under the Act, and of no others
Only facts admitted by both parties
questions.src: Section 3 BSA establishes the foundational admissibility gate, confining evidence strictly to facts in issue and relevant facts.

questions.q: "Res Gestae" (Section 4 BSA, formerly Section 6 IEA) allows admission of facts that:
o: Occurred years before the main event with no connection to it
Form PART OF THE SAME TRANSACTION as the fact in issue, even if not the fact in issue itself
Were only witnessed by law enforcement officers
Relate exclusively to the accused's character
questions.src: Res Gestae admits facts genuinely connected as part of the same transaction, even though not themselves the central fact in issue.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A confession made to a police officer is generally inadmissible under the BSA. Reason (R): This is because confessions extracted in police custody may be coerced or unreliable. Which is correct?
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) does not explain (A)
questions.src: Both statements are accurate, and (R) correctly captures the genuine policy rationale behind excluding police confessions.

questions.q: Under Section 23 BSA (corresponding to old Section 27 IEA), when a fact is discovered as a consequence of information from an accused in custody:
o: The ENTIRE confession becomes admissible without limit
So much of the information as DISTINCTLY RELATES to the fact discovered may be proved
Nothing from that information can ever be admitted
Only the police officer's written notes are admissible
questions.src: This narrow exception allows only the verifiable, discovery-linked portion of an otherwise inadmissible confession into evidence.

questions.q: In Pakala Narayana Swami v. Emperor (1939), the Privy Council held that the phrase "circumstances of the transaction which resulted in death" (dying declaration provision) is:
o: Narrowly limited to statements made in the presence of a Magistrate only
WIDER in interpretation than merely the direct cause of death, covering the broader transaction leading to it
Inapplicable to statements made to family members
Only relevant in civil proceedings, never criminal
questions.src: This landmark Privy Council ruling gave dying declaration provisions a genuinely broad interpretation, covering the wider transaction, not just the immediate cause.

questions.q: Statement 1: A dying declaration requires corroboration as a strict rule of law before it can support a conviction. Statement 2: The requirement of corroboration for a dying declaration, where applied, is a rule of prudence rather than a strict rule of law. Which is correct?
questions.src: Statement 1 is false -- corroboration is not a strict legal requirement. Statement 2 correctly reflects the settled position (Munnu Raja v. State of M.P.) that corroboration is a rule of prudence, not law.

questions.q: For a dying declaration to be admissible under Section 26(a) BSA, a key essential requirement is that the declarant:
o: Must have expected death at the time of making the statement
Must have DIED, and the statement must relate to the cause of death or circumstances leading to it
Must have made the statement exclusively to a police officer
Must have been over 60 years of age
questions.src: The declarant's death and the statement's relation to the cause/circumstances of death are essential requirements -- expectation of death is NOT required under Indian law.

questions.q: The doctrine "Nemo Moriturus Praesumitur Mentire" (Section 26 BSA / Section 32 IEA), meaning "no one at the point of death is presumed to lie," forms the basis for admissibility of:
questions.src: This maxim is the traditional rationale underlying the dying declaration exception to the hearsay rule.

questions.q: Under Section 39 BSA (corresponding to Section 45 IEA), "Expert Opinion" is relevant on a point of:
o: Any matter whatsoever, regardless of technical complexity
Foreign law, science, art, or identity of handwriting/finger impressions, where the court needs specialised assistance
Only matters already decided by a lower court
questions.src: Expert opinion is relevant specifically for technical/specialised matters requiring assistance beyond a court's ordinary knowledge.

questions.q: Under the doctrine of "Res Inter Alia Acta" (Section 40 BSA / Section 46 IEA), when an expert's opinion is relevant:
o: No other fact can ever support or contradict that opinion
Any fact SUPPORTING or CONTRADICTING that opinion also becomes relevant
Only the expert's written report matters, not oral testimony
The court must always defer entirely to the expert's conclusion
questions.src: This doctrine allows facts that support or contradict an expert's relevant opinion to also be brought before the court.

questions.q: The "Best Evidence Rule" (Sections 55, 59, 94 BSA, formerly Sections 60, 64, 91 IEA) generally requires that:
o: Only oral testimony is ever acceptable
The BEST AVAILABLE evidence be produced -- for documents, the ORIGINAL document itself
Photocopies are always preferred over originals
Witnesses must always be cross-examined twice
questions.src: This foundational evidentiary principle requires producing the most direct, original form of evidence available, particularly the original document itself.

questions.q: Under BSA, electronic records (emails, WhatsApp chats, CCTV footage, server logs) are now treated as:
o: PRIMARY evidence, with the same legal status as paper documents
Only admissible if printed and physically signed by a Magistrate
questions.src: A key BSA innovation gives electronic and digital records primary evidence status, equal to traditional paper documents.

questions.q: Under Section 57 BSA (replacing old Section 65B IEA), admissibility of electronic records generally requires:
o: A CERTIFICATE authenticating the electronic record, generally requiring signatures from the person in charge of the device AND an expert
Only a verbal assurance from the person presenting it
Approval from the Ministry of Electronics and IT
questions.src: Section 57 BSA streamlines but still requires proper certification, now generally involving both the device custodian and an expert signature.

questions.q: The doctrine "Ei Incumbit Probatio Qui Dicit Non Qui Negat" (Section 104 BSA / Section 101 IEA) means:
o: The burden of proof lies on the person who DENIES, not the person who asserts
The burden of proof lies on the person who ASSERTS, not the person who denies
No party ever bears a burden of proof
The court itself must independently investigate all facts
questions.src: This foundational burden-of-proof maxim places the burden on the party making the assertion, consistent with "he who asserts must prove."

questions.q: "Prima Facie" (Section 104 BSA / Section 101 IEA) refers to evidence that is:
o: SUFFICIENT to establish a fact "on the face of it," UNLESS disproved
questions.src: Prima facie evidence establishes a fact sufficiently on its face, subject to being rebutted by contrary evidence.

questions.q: Under the general exceptions to the rule against hearsay, statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses (Section 26 BSA) apply where the person is:
o: Merely unavailable due to a scheduling conflict
DEAD, cannot be found, has become incapable of giving evidence, or attendance cannot be procured without unreasonable delay/expense
Simply unwilling to testify for personal reasons
A minor under the age of 10
questions.src: This necessity-based exception applies to genuinely unavailable witnesses under these specified circumstances, not mere reluctance.

questions.q: The "Rule of Exclusion of Hearsay" (Section 55 BSA / Section 60 IEA) generally requires that oral evidence must be:
o: Always corroborated by at least three witnesses
DIRECT -- second-hand (hearsay) information is generally not admissible
Recorded only in writing, never given orally in court
questions.src: This foundational rule requires direct evidence from a witness with firsthand knowledge, generally excluding hearsay.

questions.q: In Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar (1998), the Supreme Court distinguished between:
o: Criminal law and civil law generally
RELEVANCY, ADMISSIBILITY, and PROBATIVE VALUE as three distinct evidentiary concepts
questions.src: This case clarified that a fact may be relevant without being admissible (e.g., privileged communications), and admissible facts may vary in their probative weight.

questions.q: "Admissions" under the BSA (Sections 15-26 area) are statements made by parties that:
o: Are automatically conclusive proof of the matter admitted
AFFECT the determination of matters in issue, though not automatically conclusive
Can never be used as evidence under any circumstances
questions.src: Admissions affect determination of issues but are not automatically conclusive -- they may operate as estoppel in appropriate circumstances.

questions.q: An admission may be proved BY OR ON BEHALF OF the person making it (an exception to the general rule) where it:
o: Was made to benefit the person's business interests
Consists of a statement of the existence of a STATE OF MIND OR BODY, made at or about the relevant time, accompanied by conduct rendering falsehood improbable
Was made in front of at least five witnesses
questions.src: This specific exception allows self-serving admissions in narrow circumstances involving contemporaneous state-of-mind/body statements.

questions.q: "Res Ipsa Loquitur" (Section 109 BSA / Section 106 IEA), meaning "the thing speaks for itself," allows:
o: Automatic conviction without any evidence whatsoever
NEGLIGENCE to be inferred from the very nature of an accident/occurrence, without requiring direct evidence
Only expert witnesses to testify in negligence cases
The burden of proof to shift permanently to the plaintiff
questions.src: This doctrine permits an inference of negligence from the circumstances of an occurrence itself, easing the evidentiary burden in appropriate cases.

questions.q: "Pater Est Quem Nuptiae Demonstrant" (Section 116 BSA / Section 112 IEA) presumes that:
o: A child born during lawful wedlock is the LEGITIMATE child of the husband
All children are automatically illegitimate unless proven otherwise
Marriage certificates are inadmissible as evidence
DNA evidence is never required in paternity disputes
questions.src: This doctrine establishes a legal presumption of legitimacy for children born during a lawful marriage, rebuttable only in specific circumstances.

questions.q: "Last Seen Theory" (Section 5 BSA / Section 7 IEA) applies when:
o: A witness saw the accused at any point during their lifetime
The time gap between the accused and deceased being last seen together, and the deceased being found dead, is SO SHORT that the possibility of another person committing the crime becomes improbable
The accused was seen fleeing a country
No witnesses are available at all
questions.src: This doctrine relies on genuine temporal proximity to create a strong inference regarding the accused's involvement, not mere prior acquaintance.

questions.q: "Corpus Delicti" (Section 6 BSA / Section 8 IEA), meaning "body of the crime," refers to:
o: The literal physical body of a murder victim only
The ESSENTIAL FACTS proving that a crime has actually been committed
A specific type of witness testimony
questions.src: Corpus delicti refers broadly to the essential factual elements establishing that an offence genuinely occurred, not merely a literal body.

questions.q: "Test Identification Parade" (Section 7 BSA / Section 9 IEA) is conducted to:
o: Test the veracity of a witness and their CAPACITY TO IDENTIFY unknown persons connected to the crime
Replace the need for any trial altogether
Only apply in civil property disputes
questions.src: A Test Identification Parade specifically verifies a witness's genuine ability to identify persons connected to the alleged offence.
